analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice lawsuit damages, limits lawyer fees, and shields implant material suppliers from most liability.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee approved the medical malpractice overhaul on a bipartisan basis in May 1995, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for medical malpractice lawsuits nationwide, overriding state laws where they give injured patients more rights. It would make punitive damages rare and hard to win, let defendants spread out payments, cut what patients can recover from other insurance sources, cap lawyers' contingency fees, and mostly exempt companies that supply raw materials for medical implants from lawsuits. It also creates some patient-safety measures, like risk management programs and public disclosure of disciplinary actions against doctors.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, health plans, and malpractice insurers would gain the most: federal limits on punitive damages, joint liability, and lawyer fees would reduce their liability exposure and insurance payouts. Companies supplying raw materials and parts for implants would be shielded from most lawsuits by patients harmed by those implants. The bill's stated purpose also includes lowering malpractice premiums and keeping care available in areas where lawsuits have driven providers away.

how_it_helps.text: Punitive damages would be awarded only on clear and convincing evidence of intent or conscious disregard of risk, and only after a separate proceeding, sharply limiting the rare cases where they are available today.

Each defendant would be liable only for their own share of pain-and-suffering and punitive damages rather than the whole award, and awards would be reduced dollar-for-dollar by payments patients already received from health insurance or other collateral sources.

Lawyers' contingency fees would be capped at about a third of the recovery, and patients would need a signed specialist report before filing, plus mandatory alternative dispute resolution before or at the start of a case.

Companies that supply raw materials and component parts for implants would generally be exempt from liability for implant injuries, with narrow exceptions, and could get frivolous claims against them dismissed with attorney fees paid by the claimant.
The bill would require states to run risk management programs for providers and insurers, and direct half of punitive damage awards to state quality-assurance funds and care for underserved areas.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence would bear the cost: smaller and harder-to-collect awards, a two-year filing deadline, a new specialist-affidavit hurdle, mandatory arbitration or mediation before court, and in some baby-delivery cases a higher standard of proof. State laws that currently give patients stronger protections could be preempted.

drawbacks.text: Patients who win legitimate cases would receive less: awards reduced by insurance payments already made, defendants no longer jointly liable for the full harm, and lawyers' fees capped, which could make it harder to find representation for smaller claims.

Punitive damages, the main penalty for willful or reckless misconduct, would be available only on clear and convincing evidence and excluded in any case without a compensatory judgment, weakening the deterrence signal to providers and insurers.

The bill would override state laws that give patients greater protections, while allowing states to opt out for actions between their own residents — a compromise that would produce a patchwork of rules depending on where a case is filed.

Supporters' core claim — that these limits would lower malpractice premiums and health care costs enough to matter to patients — was asserted in the bill's findings but is a contested policy question the bill text cannot settle.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives medical providers, insurers, and implant suppliers strong, specific liability protections, while the benefits to patients are indirect and speculative: promised lower premiums and better access, plus modest safety measures like risk management programs and public disclosure of disciplinary records. The costs to injured patients are concrete and immediate — smaller awards, new filing barriers, and preemption of stronger state protections. An honest reading is that the compensation side was written for the health care and insurance industries, with patient-safety language attached to broaden its appeal.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee held hearings, marked the bill up, and reported it favorably with amendments in May 1995, and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Mitch McConnell introduced the bill in the Senate on February 16, 1995, joined by Senator Joseph Lieberman (D) and Senator Nancy Kassebaum (R).
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which held hearings on March 28, 1995 and marked it up in April.
On May 16, 1995 the committee, chaired by Senator Kassebaum, reported the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and additional and minority views were filed with the report.

The reported version softened several provisions from the introduced bill: it dropped the fixed cap on punitive damages, made state alternative dispute resolution programs encouraged rather than mandatory, and let states opt out for lawsuits between their own residents.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 110) on May 16, 1995, and the record shows no further Senate action for the rest of the 104th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, injured patients kept their existing state-law rights to sue without federal damage limits, and trial lawyers kept full contingency fees. Physicians, hospitals, malpractice insurers, and implant-material suppliers did not get the federal protections they sought.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan (two Republicans and one Democrat) and the committee reported the bill favorably, but minority views were filed and no floor vote was ever recorded, so the partisan shape of the full Senate was never tested.

industries.note: Caps on punitive damages, offsets for collateral-source payments, and fee limits would directly shrink what insurers pay out on claims. Patients' reduced recoveries are the insurer's savings.

The bill lowers liability exposure for negligent care and, in its reported version, extends its protections to health plans sued over payment decisions. Its promised benefit to patients — lower premiums, more providers in underserved areas — is indirect, while the savings to providers and their carriers are direct.

The Biomaterials Access Assurance subtitle exempts suppliers of raw materials and components from liability for implant injuries except in narrow cases, ending their exposure to lawsuits while implant manufacturers remain liable. Patients hurt by a defective implant would have fewer parties to sue.

Contingency fee caps, a mandatory specialist certificate of merit, mandatory dispute resolution before court, and reduced recoveries would cut both the revenue and the practical viability of malpractice cases. On this bill, the plaintiffs' bar's interest runs with injured patients'.
